what_its_for: Ampicillin is an antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections. It can treat infections of the ears, nose, throat, lungs, urinary tract, stomach, and intestines. It is also used to treat certain sexually transmitted infections. It only works against bacteria — it will NOT treat colds, flu, or other viral infections.
how_to_take: Take ampicillin exactly as your doctor prescribed. Swallow capsules whole with a full glass of water. Take it on an EMPTY STOMACH — either 30 to 60 minutes BEFORE a meal or 2 hours AFTER a meal. Food can reduce how well this medicine works. Try to take it at the same times each day and finish ALL of your medication, even if you start feeling better. Stopping early can allow the infection to come back.
dosing: Your dose depends on your age, weight, and the type of infection being treated. Adults are commonly prescribed 250 mg to 500 mg every 6 hours (four times a day). Children's doses are based on their body weight and are determined by the doctor. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and do not change your dose without asking your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do NOT double up or take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store ampicillin capsules at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do NOT store it in the bathroom. If you have a liquid (suspension) form, store it in the refrigerator and use it within 7 to 14 days — check the label for the exact time. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of any unused or expired medication safely at a drug take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking ampicillin with food or milk, as this can make it less effective. Do not take antacids within 1 to 2 hours of your dose, as they can interfere with absorption. Tell your doctor if you are taking other antibiotics, blood thinners like warfarin, gout medications like allopurinol (which may increase the risk of skin rash), or birth control pills — ampicillin may reduce how well oral contraceptives work, so use a backup method of birth control during treatment. Avoid alcohol, as it can worsen side effects like upset stomach.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency help if you experience: a severe skin rash, hives, or blistering skin; swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat; trouble breathing or swallowing (signs of a serious allergic reaction); severe watery or bloody diarrhea, which could be a sign of a serious gut infection (C. difficile); yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); dark urine or unusual tiredness; seizures; or if your symptoms are not getting better after a few days of treatment.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within 2 to 3 days of starting ampicillin. However, it is very important to take the FULL course of antibiotics as prescribed — usually 7 to 14 days depending on your infection — even if you feel completely better before then. Stopping early can cause the infection to return and make it harder to treat.
special_populations: Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: Ampicillin is generally considered safe during pregnancy and is sometimes used to treat infections in pregnant women, but always tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Small amounts pass into breast milk, so tell your doctor if you are breastfeeding. Kidney Problems: If you have kidney disease, your doctor may need to adjust your dose or how often you take it. Older Adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects and may need dose adjustments. Penicillin Allergy: Do NOT take ampicillin if you have ever had a severe allergic reaction to penicillin or any other beta-lactam antibiotic (such as amoxicillin or cephalosporins). Always inform your healthcare provider of all known allergies.
